name: Aisha Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year associate at a small firm that only acts for workers, people who've been sacked or pushed out or not paid what they're owed. My day starts at about half eight with the inbox, then it's mostly reading: witness statements, pay slips, a hundred emails between a warehouse manager and HR. I draft letters before claim and help prepare bundles for the tribunal, which is the special court for work disputes. The best part is the phone call where I tell someone we think they've got a case and they go quiet, then say thank you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What wears me out is how slow I am compared to the others. My boss Ruth will turn round a letter in twenty minutes that takes me two hours, and my last review said I need to speed up. I do everything on paper first, with a pen, which drives the paralegals mad. What I like most is sitting next to a client at a hearing, even if I'm only taking notes, because you can see what it means to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at work: I told you so. Half of the profession has been talking about these tools like they're magic, and if they turn out to be a fancy spellcheck I'd be quietly pleased. Online I wouldn't post anything, I'm not really someone who does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my job and I get to learn it the way lawyers always have, by doing it badly and then less badly. The firm bought a drafting tool last spring and I've never logged in. If that's all AI ever is, nobody's going to make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, and I'd put real effort into getting faster, because that's my actual problem. I'd ask Ruth if I can sit in on more of her client calls this winter. I'd keep putting a third of my salary into savings like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, but not complete calm. I'd still have the same review hanging over me and the same feeling that I'm the slowest person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be relieved. Is there anything in your work that would still worry you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The review, yes. They want me billing more hours with fewer write-offs, and the partners keep mentioning that the other junior uses the drafting tool and gets through twice as many letters. Even a small AI could make me look worse next to him. I'm not scared of losing the job, but I don't want to be the one they quietly stop giving good cases to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say if you told him AI had fizzled out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas would laugh and say I can stop reading articles at midnight. He teaches history at a secondary school, so he's got his own fights about kids using AI for homework. We'd probably open a bottle of wine. Then he'd remind me I still need to answer my review.

say: I'd tell colleagues the AI talk was **mostly hype** and the old way of training lawyers still works.
I'd keep it **off social media** because I don't post about work online.
think: Privately I think a **plateau** means I keep my job and learn law by doing it.
My real problem is my **speed**, and a colleague using the drafting tool makes me look slower.
do: Ask my boss Ruth to let me **sit in** on more client calls this winter.
Keep saving **a third** of my salary, as I already do every month.
Work on getting **faster** at letters before claim without touching the drafting tool.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with a nagging worry about my **performance review**.
S0.quote: The firm bought a drafting tool last spring and I've never logged in.
fieldNote: Her secure money is not the issue; her **slow pace** and her review drive the unease.
She frames AI as a **status contest** with the other junior rather than a threat to the job.
Writing drafts **by hand** first is part of how she thinks, not just habit.

steps.text: Keep drafting letters before claim the usual way, pen first
Put a third of each salary payment into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules before anyone hands a worker's case to software. A sacked cleaner deserves a human who actually read her file. Online I might share things from the bar association about protecting junior training, but I'd keep my own name out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's bad for me specifically. The things I do all day, reading disclosure and drafting first versions, are the exact things AI takes first. Ruth doesn't need a slow junior to write first drafts if a machine does it in a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go and talk to the staff association at the firm, which is basically a few of us and a WhatsApp group, about getting a promise that juniors still get trained. I'd push my savings from a third to nearly half. And I'd start asking about tribunal advocacy courses, so I'm the person in the room rather than the person behind the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach, a bit. I chose law because it felt solid, and this is the first time it's felt like it might not need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paralegals, Dev especially. He does all the bundles and the scheduling and he's got a little boy. If they cut him, I'd feel complicit just by still being there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use the tools. Would that hold if the firm made them part of your review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made it part of my review, I'd log in and use it, because I'm not stupid. But I'd use it for the dull parts, like page numbers on a bundle, and I'd still write the letter myself. I know that sounds stubborn. It probably is.

say: I'd say we need **rules** before software handles a worker's case.
I'd share the **bar association's** posts on junior training, but keep my own name out of it.
think: Privately I think my daily work, **first drafts** and reading disclosure, is exactly what goes first.
A partner doesn't need a **slow junior** if a machine writes the draft in a minute.
do: Raise junior **training guarantees** with the firm's small staff association.
Raise my savings from a third to **nearly half** of my salary.
Look into **tribunal advocacy** courses so I'm the one in the hearing room.
feel: A **sick feeling**, because law no longer feels as solid as when I chose it.
S1.quote: The things I do all day, reading disclosure and drafting first versions, are the exact things AI takes first.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that her **junior tasks** are the first target, even though she avoids the tools.
Her progressive view shows in **guilt** about paralegals more than in worry about herself.
She'd use the tool only if **forced** by review, and only for the dull parts.

steps.text: Ask the firm's staff association to press for junior training guarantees
Raise monthly savings from a third to nearly half of salary
Sign up for a tribunal advocacy course next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this needs to be stopped or slowed down by governments, full stop. I'd sign every open letter going. At work I'd say to Ruth that we should be thinking about what it means for our clients, because they'll lose jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone. Not in a dramatic way, but the firm will just stop needing juniors within a year or two, and I'm the junior who's furthest behind. Hearings might still need a person standing up, but I'm not the one they'd pick to stand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd save everything I can and stop thinking about buying a flat with Jonas. I'd join the lawyers' union branch, the one most people at big firms laugh at, and go to their meetings. I'd also ask Ruth to put me on every hearing she can, so I build up the one bit that's still about a person in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. I'm twenty-seven and I thought I'd just started, and in this picture it's over before I got good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got more than a year of savings. Does that change how scary this is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes how fast I panic, not whether I do. Fourteen months of savings is a lot more than most of our clients have. Money doesn't fix the part where the thing you trained for stops existing. I spent six years getting here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a law student who asked you for advice that year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a law student to go and learn to argue in a courtroom and not to count on the paperwork years to train them. Those years were how my generation learned. In this picture, those years won't exist for the next lot of students.

say: I'd say governments must **slow it down** and sign every open letter going.
I'd tell my boss we should think about our **clients' jobs**, not just ours.
think: Privately I think the firm will **stop needing juniors** within a year or two.
Hearings may still need a person, but I'm **not the one** they'd pick to stand up.
do: Put **buying a flat** with my partner Jonas on hold and save everything.
Join the **lawyers' union** branch and go to its meetings.
Ask to be put on **every hearing** going, to build courtroom skills.
feel: **Frightened**, because the career could end before I got good at it.
Aware that my **savings** soften it, but don't fix it.
S2.quote: Fourteen months of savings is a lot more than most of our clients have. Money doesn't fix the part where the thing you trained for stops existing.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** outright, and her low skill rating makes her think she'd go first.
Her **savings** buy calm about bills but not about identity.
She reaches for **collective action** first, even naming a union she says others laugh at.

steps.text: Save every spare pound instead of buying furniture or holidays
Shelve the plan to buy a flat with Jonas next year
Join the lawyers' union branch and attend monthly meetings
Sign open letters calling on government to slow AGI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pretty much the same as the fast one, but I'd add that five years is enough time for governments to act if they want to. I'd be the person at drinks saying we should be pushing the bar association hard now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just long enough for me to get properly good at law, and then it's taken away. That's almost crueller. But it does mean I could move into advocacy and maybe have a few years in court before it reaches that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years doing the tribunal advocacy course and asking to run small hearings on my own. I'd keep saving hard and I'd volunteer at the free advice clinic on Saturdays, because people there need a human more than ever. I'd stay at the firm but tell Ruth I want the court side, not the drafting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still afraid, but with a plan, which is better. It's the difference between being pushed and walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd actually do the advocacy course and get a few years of hearings behind me. With two years I'd just be scrambling. I'd also have time to help build a union branch that's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the blame sit for you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame the companies building it and the governments that won't regulate them. And honestly some of the partners, who'd happily swap three juniors for a licence fee. Not Ruth, but some of them.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** for governments to act if they choose to.
I'd push for the **bar association** to fight for junior lawyers now, not later.
think: Privately I'd get good **just in time** to have it taken away.
Five years could still buy me some **years in court** before AI reaches that too.
do: Take the **advocacy course** in the first two years and run small hearings alone.
Volunteer at the **free advice clinic** on Saturdays.
Tell my boss Ruth I want **court work**, not drafting.
feel: **Afraid** but steadier, because there's a plan to walk towards.
S3.quote: Five years is just long enough for me to get properly good at law, and then it's taken away. That's almost crueller.
fieldNote: The longer warning gives her a **plan**, but she still expects the junior desk work to vanish.
She blames **tech companies**, government and some partners, but spares her own boss.
The Saturday **advice clinic** is about values as much as career.

steps.text: Complete the tribunal advocacy course within two years
Keep saving close to half of each salary payment
Help set up a working union branch at the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. Lawyers should use the time to write the rules for how this is used in courts and in advice. At work I'd say the firm should commit to keeping a human on every client file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one I can live with. Ten years is long enough to become a proper advocate, someone who stands up in tribunals, and that part needs a person longer than the drafting does. I'd still worry about the people coming after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth for a five-year plan to move me into hearings. I'd do the advocacy course, keep my savings where they are, and give some time to the bar association's working group on AI in courts. I'd also start using the drafting tool for bundles, but only for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think, but not frightened. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would make me try, slowly. I'd probably use the drafting tool for bundles and page numbering by the second year, because I'd have time to check what it does. I still wouldn't let it write a letter to a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture yourself in 2036. Where are you working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to be standing up in a tribunal, representing someone who got sacked by an algorithm. That would be a nice twist, if I'm honest. Maybe at this firm, maybe at a law centre that's publicly funded.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift, and lawyers should write the rules for courts now.
I'd ask the firm to commit to a **human** on every client file.
think: Privately this is the one I can **live with**, because advocacy needs a person longest.
I'd still worry about the **juniors** who come after me.
do: Ask my boss Ruth for a **five-year plan** into hearings.
Join the bar association's **working group** on AI in courts.
Start using the drafting tool for **bundles only** by the second year.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, rather than frightened.
S4.quote: I'd like to be standing up in a tribunal, representing someone who got sacked by an algorithm.
fieldNote: Time turns her from alarmed to **uneasy**, because she can reach the courtroom side first.
She'd finally try the **drafting tool**, but only for bundles and never client letters.
Her picture of 2036 is shaped by **values**: defending workers harmed by machines.

steps.text: Agree a five-year move into tribunal hearings with Ruth
Use the drafting tool for bundle page numbers by year two
Join the bar association working group on AI in courts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. What would help is a guarantee that firms keep training juniors, maybe even a rule that a qualified person has to sign off advice, and some kind of public funding for law centres so there are places to go. Money for me personally isn't the issue, it's having somewhere to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd ever use the tools. I keep saying no to the AI tools, and I think part of that is fear that I'd be bad at those too. Jonas says I treat new things like exams I might fail. He's probably right.

headlineQuote: I keep saying no to the AI tools, and I think part of that is fear that I'd be bad at those too.
portrait: A **second-year associate** at a small firm that acts only for workers in employment disputes.
Slow by her own account, she drafts **by hand** and has never logged into the firm's tool.
Her **fourteen months** of savings ease bills, but not the fear of losing a career she just started.
She moves from **uneasy** in the slow scenarios to alarmed when AGI comes in two or five years.
Her answer is **advocacy**, collective action and rules, with a slow, reluctant start on AI tools.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the firm would stop needing juniors before she gets good.
whatWouldHelp: A **guarantee** that firms keep training juniors and a qualified person signs off advice.
**Public funding** for law centres so there are still places to learn.
